title: Indian-Origin Woman Wins £6.6 Million After 23-Year Divorce Battle Exposes Husband's Hidden Fortune
excerpt: Varsha Gohil's two-decade fight against a husband who concealed £28 million has changed UK divorce law for women married to men who hide their wealth.
body:
• Varsha Gohil, 61, won a £6.6 million (approximately Rs 85 crore) settlement after a 23-year divorce battle in the UK, one of the longest in British legal history.
  • Her ex-husband Bhadresh Gohil, a solicitor, concealed a £28 million fortune and was later convicted of money laundering and sentenced to 10 years in prison.
  • The UK Supreme Court used her case to establish that spouses cannot benefit from hiding assets during divorce proceedings, creating a legal precedent.
  • The UK Court of Appeal recently ruled out further appeals, finally bringing the decades-long dispute to a close.

A Modest Settlement That Unravelled

When Varsha Gohil filed for divorce in May 2002, she had no idea her case would become one of the longest and most consequential in British legal history. After 12 years of marriage and three children, she cited adultery and unreasonable behaviour against her husband Bhadresh Gohil, a high-flying London solicitor, according to The Times.

The discovery came during an illness. Bed-bound with flu and caring for three small children and her mother-in-law, Varsha opened her husband's laptop and found emails revealing hotel bookings and exchanges that pointed to a long-term affair at a five-star resort in Goa.

The initial divorce was settled quickly in 2004. Varsha accepted £270,000 — roughly Rs 3.47 crore — and kept the family's Peugeot 206. Her husband retained two Mercedes vehicles. For Varsha, then 37, it appeared to be the end. It was, in fact, only the beginning.

Criminal Conviction Reveals Hidden Millions

Varsha grew suspicious that Bhadresh had not disclosed the full extent of his wealth during the divorce proceedings. Under UK law, both parties are required to provide a complete account of their assets when financial settlements are decided.

In 2007, she returned to court seeking to overturn the original agreement. The case took a dramatic turn when Bhadresh was investigated in connection with a money laundering operation linked to James Ibori, a former Nigerian state governor. In 2010, he was convicted of money laundering, forgery and conspiracy to defraud, receiving a 10-year prison sentence, according to the PTI news agency.

The criminal investigation revealed assets worth approximately £28 million — around Rs 360 crore — that had been hidden across multiple jurisdictions through offshore companies and client accounts. The UK Crown Prosecution Service froze these assets as part of confiscation proceedings.

"The husband's conduct is at the highest end of the scale in terms of dishonesty and its consequences."

— Justice Williams, UK High Court ruling

Supreme Court Sets Precedent

Varsha's fight to reopen her settlement reached the UK Supreme Court. In a landmark ruling, her case was heard alongside that of Alison Sharland, who had raised similar allegations about her ex-husband concealing assets. The court ruled that both women could reopen their financial settlements, establishing a legal principle that spouses cannot benefit from hiding assets during divorce proceedings.

The ruling now serves as a reference in cases involving undisclosed wealth across British courts.

Despite this legal victory, the financial dispute remained unresolved for years. The Crown Prosecution Service encountered significant difficulties tracing and recovering the hidden assets, delaying a new High Court hearing until 2023. At that hearing, Bhadresh argued that the frozen fortune was not his and should not be included in any divorce award.

A Hard-Won Resolution

Justice Williams ultimately awarded Varsha £6.6 million — approximately 23.82% of the identifiable untainted realisable assets of around £6,663,172, compared to the total realisable assets of £27,967,337 subject to the confiscation order, as detailed in his May 2025 ruling.

"The wife is now nearing retirement age and has come through the last 23 years with health problems, but financially, she is still afloat," Justice Williams noted in his judgment.

The UK Court of Appeal recently ruled out any further appeals, finally allowing the High Court judgment to take effect and bringing the decades-long saga to a close. The judgment was made in May 2025 but was not published until recently.

Lessons for the Diaspora

Varsha's case highlights the legal vulnerabilities that can arise during cross-border divorces, particularly when significant wealth is involved. For members of the Indian diaspora in the UK, the case underscores the importance of independent financial due diligence during marriage and divorce proceedings.

The precedent established by her Supreme Court case has strengthened protections for spouses in the UK, ensuring that deliberate concealment of assets cannot shield wealth from fair division. Legal professionals say the case has had a tangible impact on how divorce settlements are scrutinized when financial disclosure is disputed.

For Varsha, who largely fought her case without legal representation over two decades, the settlement represents not just financial recovery but vindication.
